title: Best tools to use for pixel art?
author: JoMaster_69
selftext:
I have middling experience in game development, but am very new to using AI to generate assets. For the purpose of top down 2D pixel art, including tilesets, animated sprites, portraits, particles, etc. what are the best AI tools I should be using? 

If anyone has additional tips on how to acclimate myself to this smoothly, I would appreciate them.

comments.author: RealAstropulse
comments.body: I mean not to toot my own horn but im gonna do just that- I'm the creator of [Retro Diffusion](http://retrodiffusion.ai). You can do pretty much everything you mention with it, and its really cheap and fast, and has a pretty simple api as well. Im always adding new stuff to it, like this month we're focusing on tilesets, with a few other features coming out as well.

comments.author: Final_Parsec
comments.body: We've had a lot of success making basic animations and static doodads then using [Unfaker](https://jenissimo.itch.io/unfaker) to clean it up and make it look closer to pixel art. Not the author, but it’s been a super helpful, free, and open source tool.

replies.body: Yeah, using nano banana then Unfaker is a great combo. You'll still need some hands on artistry to clean it up, but Unfaker will give you the sharp real pixels you need.

comments.author: gametank_ai
comments.body: I built Gametank to do just that! It utilizes an AI powered workflow so you can generate assets fast. Pick a category of asset you are trying to generate (character, tile, effects, UI, etc), genre selection would be Pixel Art in this case, and you can also select art style/perspective & more so the assets stay cohesive. We also have some guides to get you started (https://www.gametank.com/guides). Curious what vibe you are aiming for?

comments.author: Haunting_Force_9391
comments.body:
If you’re starting with pixel art for top-down games, tools like **Aseprite** and **Piskel** are great for hands-on work. For AI help, **PixelVibe**, [**Scenario.gg**](http://Scenario.gg), or **Stable Diffusion** with pixel-art models can generate good bases for tiles or sprites.

I found this guide really useful too  it lists some top pixel art creator tools and how to mix AI with manual editing: [https://www.filereadynow.com/productivity-tools/pixel-art-creator](https://www.filereadynow.com/productivity-tools/pixel-art-creator).

comments.author: Haunting_Force_9391
comments.body: You can try **Aseprite** for editing and **PixelNova** or [**MyShell.ai**](http://MyShell.ai) for AI-generated art. For quick browser-based creation, [FileReadyNow’s Pixel Art Creator](https://www.filereadynow.com/productivity-tools/pixel-art-creator) is free and easy to use.

comments.author: shubham_devNow
comments.body:
If you’re working with top-down 2D pixel art, I’d honestly suggest a mix of traditional tools + light AI support, rather than relying fully on AI generation.

For core pixel work, tools like Aseprite, Pyxel Edit, or Piskel are still hard to beat for tilesets, sprites, and animations. They give you proper control over grids, palettes, and frame-by-frame animation, which AI often struggles with in pixel-perfect workflows.

On the AI side, it’s more useful as a helper than a replacement. Some people use AI for rough concept ideas, colour palettes, or references, then clean everything up manually. If you want something more focused on pixel workflows, FileReadyNow’s Pixel Art Maker is worth a look—it’s simple, fast, and can help generate base pixel assets that you can refine inside your main editor instead of starting from scratch.

A few tips to ease the transition:

* Stick to a fixed resolution and palette early on.
* Generate small test assets first (icons, props) before trying full characters or tilesets.
* Always manually edit AI output—polish is where pixel art really shines.
* Build a reusable tileset style guide so assets stay consistent.

AI can definitely speed things up, but for pixel art, your eye and manual tweaks still do most of the heavy lifting.
